intro: Puglia's regional register recognises exactly four trees anywhere in the whole of Bari as officially monumental, and this list carries all four. Two share a flowerbed in the gardens of Piazza Umberto I outside the central station: an Argentine ombu too heavy for its own roots, and a Mexican ponytail palm locals call the smoke-eater. A third, a scarred Aleppo pine in the suburb of Carrassi, has been climbed by neighbourhood kids for decades. The fourth stands 30 kilometres out in Quasano, a Murgia hamlet, named the Lie Tree for the grievances peasants once traded beneath it.
meta_description: Bari's four officially monumental trees: an Argentine ombu, a Mexican elephant's foot, a climbed Aleppo pine, and a holm oak named for peasant grievances.
question_answer: Bari's oldest tree, by the best available evidence, is the Lie Tree of Quasano, a holm oak in the Murgia hamlet of Toritto planted in the second half of the 19th century, putting it at roughly 125 to 175 years old. The Pine of Carrassi, inside the city itself, sits in a nearly identical range, estimated at around 150 years by a University of Bari botanist who cautions that dating either tree precisely is very difficult.
question_meta: Bari's oldest tree may be the Lie Tree of Quasano, a 19th century holm oak 30km out, tied by the city's Pine of Carrassi. All 4 monumental trees.
question_context: Age here is a matter of best evidence rather than precision, because none of Bari's four officially monumental trees carries a measured planting date. The Lie Tree of Quasano has the strongest documented basis: local sources say it is absent from the estate's own land records before the mid-1800s, and its name comes from complaints peasants traded beneath it in the disillusioned years after Italian unification. The Pine of Carrassi rests on a University of Bari botanist's estimate of roughly a century and a half, given with the same caution. The two younger trees, an Argentine ombu and a Mexican ponytail palm sharing a bed in Piazza Umberto I outside the central station, are neither dateable by growth rings (both are technically giant herbs, not true trees) nor documented at planting. The Quasano tree is a genuine day trip, about 30 km from the centre with no direct rail; the other three sit within a few kilometres of Bari Centrale.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Bari?
faq.a: Probably the Lie Tree of Quasano, a holm oak roughly 125 to 175 years old in the Murgia hamlet of Toritto, though the city's own Pine of Carrassi is estimated at a very similar age and neither can be dated precisely.

faq.q: Why does Bari have so few monumental trees?
faq.a: Puglia's regional register of monumental trees recognises only four anywhere in the comune of Bari. It is a strict legal designation, not a count of every remarkable tree in the city, and this list is all four.

faq.q: Are Bari's trees free to see?
faq.a: Yes. The ombu and the ponytail palm stand in the public gardens of Piazza Umberto I, the pine on an open street corner in Carrassi, and the Lie Tree beside a public road in Quasano. None needs a ticket.
Albero della Bugia. Quasano's holm oak earned the name from the grievances peasants aired beneath it about broken promises from Italian unification's patriots, and the name outlasted the complaints.

trees.name: The Ombu of Piazza Umberto I

location.address: Giardini di Piazza Umberto I, Bari

trees.transport: Bari Centrale railway station, about 5 minutes' walk
trees.story:
Saving one of Bari's four officially monumental trees has been costed at around a thousand euros, and the money has not been spent. The tree is an ombu, it stands in the gardens of Piazza Umberto I five minutes from the central station, and it leans. It leans because it has spent years reaching for light past the holm oaks around it, and because the asphalt laid up to its base has damaged the plate of roots underneath. A local civic association put all of that in a letter to the mayor asking for a modest repair job.

The species is stranger than the tree looks. Phytolacca dioica is not a tree in the botanical sense but an outsized herb from the South American pampas, its trunk swollen with water storing tissue rather than timber, which is why nobody can date one by counting rings. Italy imported it in the middle of the 19th century as an ornamental curiosity, and almost none of those imports ever reached this size. This one is 2.5 metres around and about six metres tall, low and heavy and grey, and both the Puglia and the national registers list it as monumental on those measurements.

Its age is a guess by its own defenders, whose letter says it was probably planted in the 1950s. Nobody has put a firmer date on it. If you know one, tell us.

trees.name: The Mangiafumo of Piazza Umberto I

location.address: Giardini di Piazza Umberto I, Bari

trees.transport: Bari Centrale railway station, about 5 minutes' walk
trees.story:
Bari calls this one la mangiafumo, the smoke-eater, on the local conviction that it swallows the traffic fumes of the streets around it. That part is folklore. What is not folklore is the base: three metres around, swollen into a grey elephantine foot that stores water, sitting in a public garden two minutes from the central station.

Nolina longifolia is a Mexican plant from dry limestone slopes at altitude, and the specimens Europe planted as ornamental curiosities in its gardens almost all stayed modest. This one did not. Three metres of girth under four and a half metres of height was enough for the Puglia and the national registers to list it as a monumental tree, one of only four in the whole of Bari and one of 74 in the region. A second of those four, the ombu, stands a few metres away in the same bed, so a visitor can see half of the city's officially remarkable trees without turning around.

The gardens around it were made by merging two 19th-century ones and rebuilt in 1905 around the equestrian statue of Umberto I. The mangiafumo's own arrival went unrecorded. It lays down no countable rings and no planting date has surfaced, so it comes to this page without even a range. If you know when it went in, tell us.

trees.name: The Pine of Carrassi

location.address: Corso Alcide De Gasperi, corner of Via Ugo La Malfa, Carrassi, Bari

trees.access: Free, public roadside plot. The tree stands in a small enclosed bed behind a low concrete wall right at the street corner, visible and reachable from the pavement at any time; no gate, ticket or permission needed.
trees.transport: Carrassi district, about 3 km south of Bari Centrale station; reachable by city bus along Corso Alcide De Gasperi, no rail nearby.
trees.story:
A branch on this Aleppo pine broke off in a heavy snowfall about two decades ago, and Bari's foresters simply cut the stump flush and left the rest standing, close to six metres round at the trunk. It grows in a fenced bed on a street corner in Carrassi, behind a low concrete wall low enough that generations of neighbourhood kids have climbed over it and up the tree itself, which the local paper reports as an open secret rather than a problem anyone has stopped.

The tree is one of only four in the whole of Bari that Puglia's monumental register recognises, though even the record argues with itself about what it is: the official listing calls it an Aleppo pine, a separate botanical survey calls the same tree a stone pine, and nobody has resolved which. A University of Bari botanist puts its age at roughly a century and a half, the same estimate he gives for a second monumental tree across town, while warning in the same breath that dating either one precisely is close to impossible.

Do not confuse it with the pine that stood one intersection further along the same street and was felled in 2025. This one, at the De Gasperi corner with Via Ugo La Malfa, is still there.
trees.verify_notes: Two independent sources beyond the register: Barinedita (3 Jan 2018, in-person visit) places it exactly at the De Gasperi/Via Ugo La Malfa corner, describes a small plot enclosed by a low concrete wall, trunk split into three main branches, one branch amputated about 20 years before the 2018 article after breaking in heavy snow. Locals use the spot as a landmark (children climb it, couples meet there). Italian Botanical Heritage's English page corroborates location, girth (19 ft = approx 580 cm, matching the register's 570 cm) and rough height, but calls it a 'stone pine (Pinus pinea)' rather than the register's Pinus halepensis (Aleppo pine) - SPECIES CONFLICT, flagged rather than resolved; Barinedita's own text just says 'pino' without a species. Height also disagrees: register says 17 m, both secondary sources converge on about 13 m. Age is an estimate, not a measurement: botanist Pietro Medagli (University of Salento) is quoted giving 'roughly 150 years' for both this pine and the Carbonara leccio (candidate from the same brief, blocked separately for access), while explicitly cautioning that precise dating of either is very difficult; treat 150 as a named expert's best guess, not a derived figure. No sourced confirmation newer than the 2018 article that the tree is still standing, so flagged for that too - but note this is NOT the pine felled in June 2025 (BariToday, 13 June 2025, 'Pino storico in corso Alcide De Gasperi verso l'abbattimento'): that dead tree stood at the De Gasperi corner with Via Pende, a different intersection on the same street, confirmed by the article's own image filename and dateline.

trees.name: The Lie Tree of Quasano
trees.age_estimate: planted in the second half of the 19th century, so roughly 125 to 175 years old
trees.access: Free, standing in the open at a road junction in the centre of the Quasano hamlet; no gate, ticket or permission needed.
trees.transport: About 30 km from central Bari, no direct rail; reachable by STP's regional bus network via Toritto, or by car via the SP231, roughly 45 minutes each way. A genuine day trip rather than a city-centre stop.
trees.story:
Quasano calls its holm oak the Lie Tree. The name is a leftover complaint: after Italian unification, peasants gathered under its crown to trade grievances about promises the Garibaldian patriots had made and never kept, and the bitterness became the tree's name. Nobody recorded a planting date, but its absence from the estate's own land records before the mid-1800s land divisions is the closest thing to a birth certificate it has, putting it at somewhere over a century and a half old.

It stands exactly where it would have overheard those complaints, right in front of the gate of Quasano's old baronial masseria, positioned so awkwardly that carts once had to work around it to get through. A small chapel, later folded into a university building, faces it from across the way. At 3.2 metres round and 11 metres tall, it earned a place on Puglia's register of monumental trees in 2021, protected under the national law for trees of exceptional age, size or history. Italians have nominated it to the FAI's Places of the Heart campaign seven times since 2006, an unusually long streak of affection for a tree named after lying.

The gate it blocks now leads to nothing grander than divided smallholdings, the old estate broken up long ago. The tree outlasted the arrangement it complained about.
trees.verify_notes: Two national/regional registers agree on species, girth (320cm) and height (11m). Three independent web sources beyond the registers: FAI's fondoambiente.it page (nominated to I Luoghi del Cuore in 2006, 2010, 2014, 2016, 2018, 2020, 2022, seven times), Italian Botanical Heritage's English page (independently confirms species, girth and height in imperial units matching the metric register figures), and Toritto Online's 11 June 2021 article (confirms the tree's May 2021 regional-decree listing under national law 10/2013, quotes the designation reason as 'age, dimensions and historical, cultural and religious value'). Age is FAI's own claim, 'planted in the second half of the 19th century', supported by the absence of the tree from the estate's land records before the mid-1800s post-Murattian divisions; not a girth-derived estimate. Access: register coordinates reverse-geocode (Nominatim, 2026-08-27) to Viale della Pineta, a pedestrian way in Quasano village centre, consistent with FAI's description of the tree standing in front of the old masseria's gate, blocking cart access; a public road/square, not private grounds, clearing hard rule 10 test 1. Distance (29.8km from Bari centre) exceeds the usual ~30-minute transit guideline but is consistent with the day-trip candidates this same Bari pass already evaluated (Molfetta, 24-29km); labelled honestly as a day trip rather than presented as a city-centre stop, per the Coole Park/Galway precedent. A Commons image is linked from this tree's Wikidata entry (Q55742469, 'Leccio - Chiesa Maria SS degli Angeli di Quasano.jpg') but was not viewed or judged this pass (this runner's egress proxy blocks Wikimedia); left for a photo-viewing session, and the filename suggests it may show the nearby chapel rather than the tree itself, so it needs a careful look rather than an automatic approval.
